If you are giving advanced training or explaining a subject that is unfamiliar to people, you may want to compare it with a subject that is familiar. This is the purpose of an analogy. It is very helpful when training people in something new and unfamiliar.
We often use the grammatical construction of as ... as ...
An analogy is used when we compare something that is familiar to people with something that is less familiar, to help them understand the less familiar thing.

Example:
1. Reading Ted's handwriting is as simple as reading ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics.
(people may not know Ted or how bad his handwriting is, but most people know they cannot read ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics)

The same sentence can be reworded with the verb inside the as ... as ... construction. If the verb, object or phrase of the second clause is identical to the first clause, it is not repeated because it is understood.
2. Ted's handwriting is as simple to read as ancient hieroglyphics (understood:... is simple to read) .
It is as important to manage the health of a business as to manage personal health.
Emotional pain may be felt as intensely in a business as physical pain is experienced by a sick person.

Spoken English may be harder to understand when someone is speaking quickly because the syllables of some words may not be pronounced as they are glided over. These are called silent syllables . They occur in pronunciation when unstressed vowels are not pronounced.

images.text: Today's staff training is on business crisis management. I have looked at several models for explaining the cycle that occurs when businesses deal with crisis. It is important to remember that the pattern is cyclical. An active and growing corporate business will continue to face and deal with challenges. I would like to use a medical comparison for understanding the crisis cycle.  For success, it is as important to manage the health of a business as to manage personal health. Managing health means living in a way that prevents disease. The first step to crisis management is actually working to prevent problems.

Yet on average, people have a lot of contact with viruses. Healthy people can get sick
just as often as good businesses face problems. When this happens, we move to step two: experiencing symptoms. The symptoms of an illness are as informative for a sick person as warnings of a problem are informative to a business.

Now comes step three: diagnosis, or identification. It is as important to diagnose an illness for the right treatment as to identify the business problem for the right solution. Generally, this is a time of shock. Emotional pain may be felt as intensely in a business as physical pain is experienced by a sick person. Since pain is high, we may logically assume this is the most difficult stage in our work. Interestingly, this pain is not as difficult as the next stage.Now, when you're comfortable after your short break, please spend a moment thinking about why this may be.
